title: Let the first minute pass
idea: A strong urge often softens if you wait one minute before acting on it.
explanation: Strong reactions feel urgent because they arrive all at once. A short pause gives your thinking time to catch up, and you often choose differently.
action: Next time you feel a sharp urge to reply or snap, wait one full minute first.

title: Make it small enough to start
idea: A habit becomes easier to keep when the first step is almost too small to refuse.
explanation: Big goals often stall at the start. Shrinking the first step removes the friction, and momentum does the rest.
action: Choose one habit you've been putting off and shrink it to two minutes today.

title: Sort what is yours to control
idea: Much of our stress comes from worrying about things we cannot change.
explanation: Separating what you can influence from what you cannot brings your energy back to the things you can act on.
action: Write down one worry today, then mark whether it is within your control.

title: Decide the night before
idea: Choosing tomorrow's first step tonight removes a decision from a busy morning.
explanation: Mornings are when we have the least patience and the most distractions. A plan made in advance does the thinking for you.
action: Before bed, write down the first small thing you'll do tomorrow.

title: Make the good thing easy to reach
idea: The habits you keep are often the ones that take the least effort to start.
explanation: Put what you want to do within arm's reach, and move what you want to avoid out of sight. Your surroundings can do more of the work than willpower.
action: Move one thing you want to use every day to the place you'll see it first.

title: Know what matters most
idea: Being clear about what matters most makes everyday choices much easier.
explanation: Picture the person you want to be in five years. Then ask whether today's choices move you a little closer to them.
action: Write one sentence describing the person you're becoming.

title: Tidy one small thing
idea: Putting your immediate surroundings in order gives you a steadier base for the rest of the day.
explanation: A cluttered desk or a full sink quietly adds tension. Fixing one small thing gives you a sense of control and a clear start.
action: Tidy one surface before you leave the room.

title: Notice the story you're telling
idea: The meaning we give an event can hurt more than the event itself.
explanation: When something upsets you, ask what you're assuming. There is often a kinder, more accurate version of what happened.
action: Next time you feel hurt, write down the story you're telling yourself, then one other possible explanation.

title: Give the worry a job
idea: A worry often calms down when it's given a clear, specific task.
explanation: Anxiety feels bigger when it has no direction. A short, practical step gives the worry something useful to do.
action: When a worry comes up, write down one practical step you could take, even if you don't take it yet.

title: Find meaning in how you respond
idea: Even in hard times, meaning can come from how you choose to respond.
explanation: We cannot always choose what happens to us. We can choose our attitude and our next action, and that choice matters.
action: Write down one small way you responded well to something hard this week.

title: Ask what you would regret
idea: Remembering that time is limited can make it clearer what truly matters.
explanation: Most daily worries fade quickly. Asking what you would regret not doing helps separate the urgent from the important.
action: Tonight, name one thing you would regret not doing this month, then put it in your calendar.

title: Choose what gets your time
idea: You cannot do everything, so it helps to choose deliberately what deserves your time.
explanation: Trying to keep up with every demand leaves no room for what matters. Accepting your limits can make your time feel more meaningful.
action: Pick one thing you won't do this week, and let it go or say no to it.

title: Pause before the purchase
idea: Money is most useful as freedom, not as a way to prove something to others.
explanation: Spending to impress rarely brings lasting satisfaction. Real wealth often shows up as the choices you no longer have to make.
action: Next time you feel the urge to buy something new, wait 48 hours and ask whether it adds to your freedom.
